messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Marco R.

Marco R. was fifty-three when the police stopped him on a Tuesday evening in late October, three years ago. He had been driving home from his office in downtown Miami after a long day of reconciling corporate tax filings—work that usually steadied him, gave him something concrete to hold. The officer who approached his window was young, maybe twenty-five, with his hand already moving toward his belt. Marco, who had grown up in this city, whose parents had come from Puerto Rico with nothing, knew the script. He kept his hands visible. He spoke softly. He did everything right.

The beating came anyway. It came fast and without warning, as though his compliance had been irrelevant from the start. The officer's partner joined in. Marco remembered the sound of his own ribs cracking, the taste of blood, the way his vision narrowed to a single point of light before everything went dark. When he woke in the hospital, his left arm was fractured in two places. The stitches across his cheekbone would leave a scar that he still touches sometimes, as if checking that it is still there. The official report said he had "resisted." The charges were eventually dropped. No one was disciplined.

For the first weeks afterward, Marco functioned. He returned to work after six weeks, moving carefully through the office in a way his colleagues pretended not to notice. But by November, something had shifted in how he moved through the world. He began avoiding the routes he used to take to the office, steering away from any street where he had seen a police car. He stopped going to the grocery store on Saturday mornings when it was crowded; the thought of being in an unfamiliar place where he could not quickly assess who was around, where he could not see the exits clearly, made his chest tighten. He could not explain this to himself in language that made sense—only that he needed to know where danger might come from before he entered a space. He began identifying escape routes in every room he entered, tracing them mentally the way other men might scan a menu. At the gym, he positioned himself near the door. At client meetings, he sat where he could see the hallway.

What frightened Marco most, though, was not the fear itself but what the fear meant about him. He had come to believe that something intrinsic to him—something in his bearing, his skin, his very presence—had invited that violence. If he had been someone else, someone less marked by his own history, perhaps the officer would have seen a man instead of a threat. This thought, once it took hold, would not release him. When he caught his reflection unexpectedly, he would see the scar and feel a surge of shame so acute it nearly stopped his breath. He began to isolate himself, declining invitations from colleagues, letting his friendships attenuate into polite text messages that grew further apart. His ex-wife called once to check on him; he did not call back. He had come to feel set apart from other people in a way he could not bridge, as though the trauma had marked him as fundamentally different, fundamentally wrong.

The isolation deepened his hypervigilance. With fewer people in his life to anchor him to normalcy, Marco's mind had more room to work. He scrolled through news reports of police shootings, each one landing like a confirmation of his own vulnerability. When he saw footage of an injured person—a man with a bandaged face, a woman with visible bruising—something in his nervous system would spike. The image would pull him back into that Tuesday evening, and he would feel the phantom pain in his ribs, the pressure in his chest. These moments of contact with others' injuries, with reminders of victimization, would send him spiraling into deeper conviction that the world was fundamentally unsafe and that he was fundamentally unable to protect himself. The checking behind him intensified. The mental mapping of exits became obsessive. He began sleeping with his bedroom door locked and a flashlight on the nightstand.

By the time Marco came to his first session three months ago, his work had begun to suffer. He had missed two important client meetings, citing illness. His supervisor had started asking questions. He sat in the office with his shoulders pulled tight, his eyes tracking the window, and said quietly that he did not know how much longer he could do this—not the work, not any of it. He was not sure his life was worth living anymore, and he meant it in a way that frightened him. What he wanted most was to feel safe again, to trust that he could walk into a room without mapping every exit, to look at another person's scar without feeling his own wounds reopen.

violation_explanations: The vignette describes triggers (police cars, crowded spaces, images of injured people) and negative appraisals (beliefs that something intrinsic to him invited violence, that he is fundamentally different/wrong) but does not establish a causal connection within any single paragraph showing that exposure to triggers drives or leads to these negative appraisals.
